deep-tech-ca2c2127c3.headline: Nvidia results beat expectations, as ousted CEO Huang told no way back
deep-tech-ca2c2127c3.fulltext:
Search the way you think. Try our AI-powered search to find news faster.
US chip giant Nvidia doubled revenue in the third quarter to more than US$115 billion, the company reported on Tuesday while ruling out any return for ousted CEO Jensen Huang after a Chinese spy scandal.
The results, which beat expectations, came hours after Huang said he wanted his job back in the latest twist for the company at the centre of an AI boom that has propelled markets to record highs and boosted global economic growth.
Huang, a leading promoter of AI, stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a spy for Beijing.
Investors scoured the upbeat results for evidence that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” interim CEO Colette Kress said in a statement, her first since being appointed by the board last week.
She forecast stronger revenue growth of 75 per cent in next financial year, up from 70 per cent.
The recent upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia – which has lost US$700 billion in market value since the scandal broke – and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.
But his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and others for his return, and even US President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the espionage allegations.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in his first statement since his resignation.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
But Harvey Jones, the chair of the company’s board, slapped down the move, saying in an earnings call that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.
As the scandal deepened, Washington on Monday announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing.
The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.
The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.
The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.
His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying: “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”

ai-3ddd561d3d.headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B as it looks to take drug candidates to clinical trials
ai-3ddd561d3d.fulltext:
Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery platform that was spun out of Google’s DeepMind in 2021, has raised $5 billion in a Series C funding round as it seeks to take its drug candidates to clinical trials.
The funding was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with new investor Andreessen Horowitz and other investors also participating. All of the company’s existing backers, including Alphabet’s venture divisions GV and Capita G, Thrive Capital, MGX, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, also invested.
Isomorphic Labs builds an AI drug-design engine that uses a slew of simulation AI models that explore various areas of chemistry to help the company design drugs. The company, whose work builds on DeepMind’s breakthrough AlphaFold protein-folding AI model, said its program has yielded “positive preclinical results” in oncology and immunology. The lab has struck deals with pharma giants like Eli Lilly, Novartis, and Johnson & Johnson.
The new funding, which comes on the heels of a $2.1 billion Series B round in May, will be used to continue developing its drug-design engine, as well as to foray into more types of medicine.
The Series C is Isomorphic’s first fundraise since its founder and CEO, Demis Hassabis, left his position as head of DeepMind to focus on drug discovery, which also saw him moving into a chairman role at DeepMind. Hassabis and then-director of DeepMind John Jumper won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the lab’s work on AlphaFold, a system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins with nothing more than their genetic sequence.
Isomorphic did not disclose its new valuation. Bloomberg reported earlier this month that the lab was looking to raise funding at a $50 billion valuation.

indian-startups-62b087555d.headline: Sarvam AI Opens Token Factory To Run Global AI Models On Indian Servers
indian-startups-62b087555d.fulltext: AI unicorn Sarvam AI has opened Token Factory to developers and enterprises, giving them access to its own and global AI models through a single application programming interface (API). The company runs the models on GPU clusters in India. Token Factory hosts Sarvam 105B alongside global open-weight models including Google’s Gemma 4 31B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3.1 Pro. Developers can switch between supported models through the OpenAI-compatible API without setting up their own computing infrastructure. The platform charges customers based on the number of tokens they send to a model and the number it generates in response. Sarvam’s catalogue lists Sarvam 105B at ₹15 per Mn input tokens and ₹60 per Mn output tokens. Cached input tokens cost ₹5 per Mn. Sarvam claimed Token Factory matches or beats leading global inference providers on speed and cost for most of the models it hosts. In the company’s tests, Sarvam 105B returned its first token in 200 milliseconds and generated 330 tokens per second for a single user. The company said it serves more than 450 Bn tokens a day on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. The three-tier cache reduces the computation needed when parts of a prompt repeat. Sarvam first outlined its plans to run its own and global open-weight models on India-based infrastructure at its Sarvam Epoch event earlier this year. It announced general availability for Token Factory earlier this month. Competition In Local Inference Krutrim began hosting DeepSeek models on Indian servers in January 2025. OpenAI introduced India-based API inference for eligible GPT-6 Luna workloads on November 12, while Anthropic offers in-country inference for select Claude models through Amazon Bedrock. In the broader inference market, Sarvam will compete with Together AI and Fireworks AI, which provide managed infrastructure for running open-weight models, and OpenRouter, which gives developers access to hundreds of models through one API. Cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud also offer model hosting and inference services. Sarvam’s pitch to enterprises is that they can switch between its own model and several global open-weight models through one API while keeping prompt processing in India. Sarvam says it runs those models on its own GPUs, so requests stay on its infrastructure without being routed to the model developers’ overseas APIs. For banks and other financial institutions that need to process certain workloads in India, local hosting could help address data residency requirements. Token Factory also offers dedicated GPU capacity, and Sarvam deploys its inference software on premises for critical institutions.

india-deep-tech-c2ed2ed811.headline: Semiconductor Startup Bharat Semi Raises $24 Mn Seed Funding
india-deep-tech-c2ed2ed811.fulltext:
The company is targeting initial commercial production in 2027 and claims its integrated chip technology could reduce imaging system costs by at least 70 per cent
                        
Semiconductor startup Bharat Semi has raised $24 million (approximately Rs 215 crore) in seed funding to develop artificial intelligence (AI)-powered image sensors, as it looks to advance its chip technology and expand into international markets.
Founded in late 2021, the company is developing programmable image sensors that integrate image capture, processing and AI capabilities into a single chip. It plans to commence initial commercial production in 2027 and is exploring opportunities in the US and other global markets.
Conventional camera systems typically use image sensors to capture visual information, which is subsequently transferred to separate processors for image processing and analysis. Bharat Semi aims to consolidate these functions into a single chip, enabling devices to interpret visual information without relying on multiple hardware components.
The startup estimates that its integrated technology could reduce imaging system costs by at least 70 per cent compared with conventional configurations that use separate image sensors, image signal processors (ISPs) and system-on-chip (SoC) components.
The company has reportedly secured design wins with US defence technology company General Atomics and Indian semiconductor manufacturer Kaynes Semicon. However, its image sensors are still under development, and Bharat Semi has not yet started generating revenue.
The startup intends to operate on a fabless business model, outsourcing semiconductor manufacturing while focusing on chip design, software development and technology innovation.

climate-energy-c53c778baa.headline: Amazon to invest $7 billion in renewable energy in India

Amazon to invest $7 billion in India renewable energy by 2030, unveils 4 new projects
New Delhi, Amazon on Tuesday announced plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, expanding its clean energy footprint in one of its fastest-growing markets.
The company has unveiled four new utility-scale renewable energy projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts (MW).
These projects include a 234 MW wind project in Karnataka which Amazon described as its largest wind energy project in Asia to date, a 200 MW hybrid wind-solar facility in Karnataka, a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh and a 200 MW solar installation in Rajasthan.
The projects are being developed through long-term power purchase agreements and will lift Amazon's contracted renewable energy capacity in India to more than 2 gigawatts (GW) once fully operational.
According to the company, the projects will generate enough electricity annually to meet the needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households.
In addition, the fresh investment comes on top of about $4 billion already committed to renewable energy projects in India.
However, the company recently set a goal of reducing the carbon intensity of electricity used across its operations by 65 per cent by 2030 compared with 2019 levels as part of its target of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.
"Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained collaboration and underline our long-term commitment to supporting India's clean energy ambitions," said Kara Hurst, Amazon's Chief Sustainability Officer.
Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi welcomed the announcement, saying such investments strengthen India's energy security, support sustainable economic growth and demonstrate global investor confidence in the country's renewable energy sector.
Moreover, Amazon currently operates 57 renewable energy projects in India, including 14 utility-scale wind and solar facilities and 43 rooftop solar installations across its operations.
Apart from its green energy push, Amazon highlighted progress in water conservation and sustainable packaging initiatives in India, including achieving water-positive status in 2025 and increasing the use of reduced packaging for customer deliveries.

deep-tech-bde2db6342.headline: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
deep-tech-bde2db6342.fulltext:
Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
Iran claims drone strike on US radar was retaliation for alleged airspace violations by US military drones.
Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive.
The military said in a statement on X on Tuesday that “any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks”.
The US earlier carried out several attacks on Iran’s southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain.
“The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas,” Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency on Tuesday.
He said the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening.
A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran’s earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain.
US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain “were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel”.
Bahrain attack
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a “precision operation” with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, in response to “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency.
It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days after a lull of several weeks. Friday’s strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported. Reuters said it came after a Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, mostly Shia clerics, to life in prison for allegedly colluding with Iran.
Kuwait’s armed forces said on Tuesday night that its air defences were responding to “hostile drone attacks” and urged the public to follow safety instructions.
It did not say where the drones came from or whether there were casualties or damage.
Tankers hit in Hormuz
Iran’s armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday. The US military says it cleared the main routes of mines.
Since the war began on February 28, Iran has tried to restrict traffic through the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, insisting that ships use only routes it has authorised. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers.
Another tanker, the Panamanian-flagged Tara Gas, was struck on Monday about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, causing a fire in its engine room, according to the security firm Vanguard.
Vanguard and India’s ports minister initially said all 25 crew, 24 of them Indian, were safe. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit a second time and the crew were “currently unaccounted for”. India’s ports minister later said the crew had abandoned the vessel after a second attack and that one Indian sailor was missing. Another Panamanian-flagged tanker, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast on Monday.
Ongoing diplomacy
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, discussed safeguarding shipping and diplomatic options in Muscat, Oman’s news agencies said.
A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East on Monday, and US President Donald Trump is due to hold a three-way summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

ai-8a57a94289.headline: Google Begins Rolling Out Personal AI Assistant, Tasks, In India
ai-8a57a94289.fulltext: Big tech giant Google has begun rolling out its new agentic AI assistant Tasks, formerly Gemini Sparks, to users in India. In a blogpost, Josh Woodward, the vice-president of Google Labs and the Gemini app, said that the new feature will enable users to assign tasks to the AI assistant, including making calls, booking appointments, comparing products and completing purchases. The service comes bundled for free with Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. “Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model,” said Woodward. It is pertinent to note that Tasks was reportedly initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, an agentic AI helper. It was subsequently expanded to the US-based subscribers of the Google AI Ultra tier. Google is now rolling out this feature for free in six markets. Unlike Gemini’s Chat that only generates responses to a user’s queries, Tasks goes one step further and enables the chatbot to perform basic functions. With the rollout, Google could be looking to expand the role of AI assistants beyond answering questions to embedding them in daily life. In his blog post, Woodward noted that Gemini can draw on information already available within Google services, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, files and payment cards, to carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. With Tasks, he also said that Gemini can call businesses, wait through hold periods, identify available appointment slots and add bookings to a user’s calendar. Under the hood, Gemini uses the agent payments protocol (AP2) to enable Tasks to make purchases online. Going forward, the big tech giant said that it plans to integrate the universal commerce protocol (UCP) into Gemini to further streamline the checkout experience. Google also said that it is working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to enable tokenised card transactions via Tasks. However, the big tech juggernaut did not specify whether partnerships extend to India too. That said, India’s inclusion in the initial rollout gives Google a large market to test consumer adoption of the personal AI assistant feature. To further scale the rollout, Google has also invited app developers to join its Connected Apps Platform, which could pave the way for Indian consumer, fintech, travel tech and foodtech brands to build task-based third-party integrations with the assistant. These features could make Gemini Tasks a channel for online shopping, bill payments and routine purchases. However, adoption will depend on the availability of supported merchants, payment methods and third-party apps in the country. There appears to be no clarity on this front. The launch is part of a broader wave of big tech giants rolling out personal AI assistants to capture the masses. In September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg showcased the company’s new offering called Muse, which allows an AI agent to send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. Prior to this, OpenAI also introduced Dots that can draft board meeting decks, conduct background research, and handle multi-step project management. xAI has also been developing Grok Bot, which sees cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. Microsoft is also pursuing agents, built on OpenClaw, which can function as digital teammates. Back home, Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform, launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps.

ai-9195fb7d09.headline: India's AI data centre expansion faces internal electrical bottlenecks: Fluke study
ai-9195fb7d09.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: India’s ambitions to become a major hub for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre infrastructure face significant operational hurdles, according to a new Fluke Corporation study. While operators look to scale capacity, gaps in internal electrical systems are emerging as a critical bottleneck for deploying higher-density AI workloads.Fluke commissioned the study on behalf of Censuswide, which surveyed 1,300 data centre operators and professionals across India, the US, the UK, Germany, France, and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. In India, 75% of operators experienced electrical or power-system issues in the past year.Furthermore, only 23% of Indian data centre operators consider their existing electrical infrastructure fully prepared for higher-density AI workloads. These findings highlight growing pressure on facility infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates and computing demands become increasingly power-intensive.External supply constraints are compounding these internal challenges, with 79% of Indian operators stating that access to sufficient power and grid capacity moderately or severely limits expansion. Operators report an average 13-month wait to secure additional grid connections or power capacity for AI and GPU-related growth."The industry has spent years asking where the power will come from. But our findings show that the focus should also be on how effectively data centres can use the power they already have," said Parker Burke, president of Fluke. "As AI drives unprecedented demand for computing capacity, the electrical infrastructure inside data centres is becoming a critical bottleneck. Without addressing this last-mile challenge, the industry risks having the power to expand, but not the infrastructure to deliver."Operational disruptions are already impacting deployment timelines across the sector. Nearly one-third (31%) of Indian operators report that power-quality issues, such as voltage fluctuations, harmonics, and electrical disturbances, have reduced their ability to deploy or operate high-density AI or GPU workloads.Additionally, 23% of operators noted that electrical problems are identified only after performance degradation, equipment failure, or downtime has already occurred. This reactive posture underscores the need for continuous power-quality monitoring, thermal inspections, and preventive maintenance to curb unplanned outages.On the monitoring front, 53% of Indian operators report comprehensive or extensive real-time visibility across critical electrical systems, placing the country ahead of the 45% global average. However, the report notes that operators must build upon these capabilities to detect faults before they disrupt operations.Workforce constraints present another hurdle to scaling capacity. More than half of Indian operators (56%) say recruiting qualified electrical technicians has become more difficult, while 31% report that electrical skills shortages have delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity."Grid constraints are largely outside an operator's control. What is within their control is how effectively they monitor, maintain and manage the electrical infrastructure they already have," Burke added. "Greater visibility into electrical systems and a proactive approach to maintenance will be increasingly important as operators look to maximize existing capacity, reduce disruption and support growing AI demand."

deep-tech-1cc4977211.headline: China’s ‘token export’ ambitions take shape with new Huawei-powered data centre
deep-tech-1cc4977211.fulltext:

China has set its sights on becoming an export hub for artificial intelligence computing power, as the country launches its first AI computing cluster powered by Huawei Technologies’ latest Ascend 950DT chips that specifically targets overseas customers.
The facility, which is based in the southern coastal city of Shantou, runs on the home-grown Ascend 950DT chip and is designed for a “token export” business model, according to local media reports. It started operations last week.
The 1 billion yuan (US$150 million) project is a collaboration between Huawei and several other Chinese companies. It is located at state telecoms giant China Telecom’s submarine cable landing station and is operated by IT services firm Guangdong Tianyima Information Industry.
The cluster processes AI queries from foreign users locally, with only the generated tokens transmitted back across the border, local media reported.
The project marks the latest step in China’s efforts to build out cutting-edge AI infrastructure using home-grown technology and become a global exporter of AI tokens – units of data consumed by AI models.
Huawei’s Ascend AI chips, seen as China’s best hope for cutting reliance on US semiconductors, are playing a critical role in this initiative.
The project comes as the US Commerce Department moves to tighten restrictions on Chinese companies’ access to advanced chips via overseas data centres, which is adding urgency to China’s need to boost self-sufficiency in chip technology.
Chinese AI developers have seen rapid growth in overseas demand for their models this year, as they capitalise on their lower prices compared with their Western rivals. MiniMax, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, StepFun, DeepSeek and Xiaomi have all intermittently ranked near the top of the global league table for token usage.
The new data centre also underscores Huawei’s accelerating commercial deployment of its supernode computing clusters.
The Ascend 950DT, which was launched earlier this year, features an independent architecture boasting 144 gigabytes of in-house high-bandwidth memory, delivering 1 petaflop of FP8 computing power per card.
In September, a massive Ascend 950DT supernode computing cluster – which can accommodate up to 1,024 cards and liquid-cooling technologies – went live in Shanghai under a partnership with the local unit of China Telecom, marking the first step in the commercialisation of Ascend 950DT-based data centres.
AI unicorn DeepSeek is reportedly planning to deploy at least 160,000 of the Ascend 950DT chips at a data centre in China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, according to a Bloomberg report in September.
Ann Cao is a Shanghai-based technology reporter for the Post, covering technology start-ups and policies in the city and eastern China. She graduated from the University of Hong Kong with a master's degree in journalism.

deep-tech-b85340a45a.headline: US details criminal probe into Nvidia customer Megaspeed over potential chip diversion
deep-tech-b85340a45a.fulltext:

The US Justice Department is leading a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, over possible violations of US chip export controls, US authorities said on Monday.
The Commerce Department opened its investigation in 2024 after officials detected suspicious activity while monitoring for possible diversion of sensitive semiconductors, the Commerce and Justice departments said in a joint statement. Investigators requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 on direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Nvidia placed the company on its “no sell” list the following month, the departments said.
US export-control officials worked with Singaporean law enforcement to conduct an on-site check that June, when then-CEO Alice Huang was interviewed, according to the statement. The Justice Department took the lead in the criminal investigation after the visit.
The departments said they rarely comment on ongoing investigations. They cited the “significant public attention” on the Megaspeed case in the past week as the reason for releasing details to “provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting”.
The disclosure comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his reported relationship with Alice Huang. Singapore’s own investigation into possible false declarations involving server purchases began in February 2025 and remains open, its Ministry of Home Affairs said last week.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the joint statement on Tuesday.
In a statement to the South China Morning Post on Sunday, the company said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and had hired outside lawyers to carry out an internal investigation. It said Alice Huang left on August 30, 2025, and no longer had a role there.
Howard Liu is a Beijing-based technology and business reporter at the South China Morning Post, covering the semiconductor industry, AI and global tech supply chains. Previously at Caixin Media, he focused on China’s AI, semiconductor and cloud computing sectors. A graduate of Columbia University, he enjoys running, swimming and hiking.

deep-tech-0433d3b1af.headline: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
deep-tech-0433d3b1af.fulltext:
NOV. 17, 2026
Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.
To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.
Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon showed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it plans the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.
Hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.
A fast, capable model is only half the story. Building a robot application has always meant gluing together drivers, calibration scripts, simulators, perception code, and a UI, which requires robotics expertise and a lot of time. The new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity packages that work into skills Gemini can use on your behalf:
- Robot bring-up: Installs drivers, discovers cameras, calibrates the arm, and verifies safe motion, starting from a USB cable.
- MuJoCo in Antigravity: Builds and previews simulated scenes and assets inside Antigravity, so you can try ideas in sim before touching hardware.
- Perception and control: Uses Gemini’s spatial understanding to find objects, plan grasps, and control the robot in a closed loop.
- Application building: Leverages Gemini’s coding skills to generate the controller, simulation, and complete a full Real-to-Sim-to-Real application development in a seamless, one-stop shop environment.
With the Antigravity Robotics plugin, it just takes one prompt to start rendering a MuJoCo scene

indian-startups-168a5c8c54.fulltext:
India’s deeptech funding record faces a test of scale: Speciale Invest
India’s deeptech funding hit $914 million in 2025, but limited growth capital, manufacturing dependencies and weak commercialisation pathways continue to hinder startups from scaling.
India’s deeptech companies raised $914 million in 257 rounds in 2025, 34 times the 2016 level. The harder test is turning research and prototypes into commercial products, notes Speciale Invest’s report, India’s Deep Tech Revolution - From the Lab to Growth and Exits.
Using Tracxn data through August 31 2026, the study covers 8,293 private companies worldwide, including 482 in India. India accounted for 12.8% of deeptech funding rounds in 2025 but received 1.6% of the capital.
For every 100 seed rounds, India had 23 Series A or B rounds, against 105 globally. Separately, there was one late-stage or private-equity round per 100 Indian seed rounds, against 26 worldwide. Both measures point to funding thinning as companies mature.
Sectoral advantages are uneven. Space firms can tap ISRO testing facilities and suppliers, while life-sciences ventures can draw on India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing base. Private participation in space has widened since 2020 reforms. Registered space startups rose from one in 2014 to about 440 by August 2026.
In July, Skyroot’s Vikram-I became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit from Indian soil. It was a milestone, though one launch does not establish a repeatable commercial business.
The report says battery makers still rely on imported cells and materials. Separately, Exide commissioned phase one of a 6 GWh Bengaluru cell plant in September. Semiconductor developers remain reliant on overseas fabrication and packaging. Semicon 2.0, approved in July with Rs 1,27,500 crore, aims to expand domestic capacity; the first fab is due in 2028.
The six-year Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Scheme aims to finance high-risk technology. By July 2026, the Technology Development Board had approved 22 projects with Rs 2,192 crore in support. Assistance is mainly through low-interest long-term loans, equity and equity-linked instruments, rather than standard grants.
Turning a successful pilot, or customer trial, into an order remains difficult. Vishesh Rajaram, managing partner at Speciale Invest, said, “Large companies and public-sector buyers can help turn those trials into commercial orders by agreeing upfront on what a pilot must prove and when they’ll make a purchase decision. A first order lets a startup plan production and commit to suppliers.”
Growth capital is smaller too. Indian Series A and B rounds averaged $11.5 million from January to August 2026, against $55.5 million globally, said Vishnu Rajeev, investment partner at Speciale Invest.
“That gap matters when a founder needs to qualify a product with a major customer or commission a production line before commercial revenue is predictable, Rajeev adds. He argues funding should match milestone costs, with project finance once customers make firm commitments.
The report urges faster funding decisions, shared testing facilities, more domestic Series B and C investors, and plant finance before pilots end. It also considers listings, acquisitions, licensing and secondary share sales as exit routes.
Deeptech needs not just research funding, but reliable customers and patient growth capital.

india-deep-tech-ad8e88fef3.fulltext:
New Delhi: The Indian Air Force (IAF) expects to receive its first squadron of the crucial indigenous Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) jets, whose deliveries have been delayed, by the end of March 2027 at the latest, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said on Monday.
“Very shortly, we will have LCA [Tejas] Mk1A joining [the] Indian Air Force. Within this financial year, we will have a squadron. Then we will continue developing; we will take it further… LCA [Tejas] Mark-2 will roll out maybe next year. And we are working very hard also for AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft),” said the Air Chief Marshal in response to a question at a media summit in New Delhi.
An IAF squadron typically comprises 18 aircraft, and the force has ordered a total of 180 Tejas Mk1A jets. The IAF is currently at its lowest strength in 60 years, with 29 active fighter squadrons against a sanctioned strength of 42.
ThePrint was the first to report last week that the first one or two Tejas Mk1A jets are likely to be handed over to the IAF early in 2027, possibly as soon as January.
#WATCH | ANI National Security Summit 3.0 | Delhi: On when can we see the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) fighter jets getting inducted, Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit says, "Creating indigenous capability in fully designed, developed,… pic.twitter.com/azZg5aA4CC
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
Also Read: R&AW is being blamed in Bangladesh for air force pilot’s death. It’s a red herring
Why have deliveries been delayed?
State-run aerospace and defence company Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) missed its original February 2024 deadline to begin deliveries of the first batch of 83 Mk1A jets, contracted in February 2021 for Rs 36,400 crore. The delay was primarily attributed to the late delivery of F404-IN20 engines by US manufacturer GE Aerospace.
The project was also affected by the complex process of integrating weapons and other systems. Deliveries of this first tranche were originally scheduled to be completed by February 2028.
In September 2025, HAL received a second order for 97 Mk1A aircraft, worth over Rs 62,370 crore. Deliveries under this contract are expected to begin in financial year 2027-28 and be completed over six years.
The Mk1A is an upgraded version of the indigenous Tejas Mk1 which is already operational with the IAF. Classified as a 4.5-generation fighter, it is equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, which lets it scan faster, track several targets at once, detect adversaries from longer distances and resist jamming better.
The aircraft is also equipped with beyond-visual-range (BVR) missiles, allowing pilots to engage enemy aircraft from greater distances. Its electronic warfare suite protects it against adversary sensors and weapons.
The Tejas Mk2 is envisaged as a more advanced and heavier variant, powered by more powerful GE engines. However, its prototype has yet to take its first flight.
The AMCA, meanwhile, is India’s stealth combat aircraft under development. It is being pursued through an industry partnership model, and the process of selecting the company or consortium that will help develop and build its prototypes is underway.

india-888d174911.headline: ‘Peace through strength’: Albanese and Trump hail progress on Quad alliance
india-888d174911.fulltext:
Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

world-2df6e49f02.fulltext:
[Text below is India Today's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Ukraine blows up Putin's prized Crimea bridge days before meeting with Trump, Xi
Ukraine used drones and cruise missiles to cripple the Crimea Bridge after a seven-stage operation. The strike disrupted a strategic Russian supply route ahead of Putin's talks with Trump and Xi.
Days before Russian President Vladimir Putin's high-profile talks with his American and Chinese counterparts, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, Ukraine has delivered a humiliating blow to one of Moscow's most prized infrastructure projects. Ukrainian drones and missiles have crippled the bridge connecting Crimea to mainland Russia by destroying a major section of the road bridge over the Kerch Strait in overnight operation.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike an "unprecedented operation", saying it had taken weeks of planning and involved systematically weakening Russian defences before targeting the bridge. Images and videos shared by showed the damaged section's remains submerged in the sea.
"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges," Zelenskyy said. "We are ... reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began."
The attack is particularly significant given the bridge's importance to Russia's occupation of Crimea and its military operations in Ukraine. It also comes at an awkward moment for Putin, who is preparing for high-profile talks with Trump and Xi in China's Shenzhen on Thursday, where the war is expected to feature among the discussions.
SEVEN-STAGE OPERATION TO BRING DOWN BRIDGE
According to Zelenskyy, the operation was the culmination of a seven-stage military and security campaign aimed at dismantling Russian defensive capabilities around the strategically important crossing. Ukrainian forces gradually targeted Russian air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other military installations before moving towards the final objective.
Several types of Ukrainian drones, alongside domestically developed Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles, were deployed during what Zelenskyy described as a pivotal phase of the operation.
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said its forces had spent a month systematically suppressing Russian air defence capabilities to create an opportunity for the strike. The agency said the operation demonstrated that Russian military installations in occupied territory were not beyond Ukraine's reach, despite Moscow's efforts to protect them.
The damage appeared considerably more extensive than in previous Ukrainian attacks on the crossing. While the road section suffered a major collapse, the parallel railway section also came under attack, although its supporting structure remained standing.
Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed head of Crimea, said two people had been killed in the attack and road traffic across the bridge had been suspended. Railway services partially resumed after an initial disruption.
WHY THE CRIMEA BRIDGE MATTERS TO RUSSIA
The 19-km Crimean Bridge is one of the most prominent symbols of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, when Moscow seized the Black Sea peninsula from Ukraine. Personally inaugurated by Putin in 2018, the bridge connects the Russian mainland with the peninsula through the Kerch Strait. It carries both road and rail traffic and was once a crucial supply route for Russian troops operating in southern Ukraine.
The crossing represents Moscow's attempt to cement its control over territory internationally recognised as part of Ukraine.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the structure since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. A truck bomb in October that year killed four people and forced restrictions on traffic for several months. Another attack in July 2023 destroyed a section of the road bridge, killing a couple travelling by car.
However, the latest strike appears to have inflicted more extensive structural damage, raising questions about how quickly Russia can restore the crossing.
The military consequences could be substantial, particularly for the movement of fuel, ammunition and other supplies into Crimea. Although Russian forces have increasingly relied on a land corridor running through occupied parts of southern and eastern Ukraine, the bridge remains an important alternative route.
KREMLIN VOWS TO REBUILD, BUT REPAIRS COULD TAKE TIME
Moscow has sought to play down the long-term implications of the attack. Russia's Presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin had been briefed on the incident and that the bridge would be rebuilt "even better than before".
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said a government commission had convened to assess the damage, determine repair requirements and examine alternative arrangements for transporting cargo to Crimea. However, the scale of the destruction could make restoration difficult, particularly with Ukraine retaining the ability to launch further attacks.
Finnish military analyst Emil Kastehelmi suggested the damage could have lasting consequences for Moscow's use of the crossing.
"The road bridge won’t be repaired during this war ... Ukraine has achieved a victory with both concrete and symbolic implications," he wrote on X.
Russia also faces logistical challenges in maintaining supplies to the peninsula while the bridge remains unusable. A land corridor through Russian-occupied areas of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions offers an alternative. However, Ukraine has increasingly targeted transport infrastructure in and around northern Crimea, including routes near Chongar, complicating Russian supply operations.
The damage could also have implications beyond the battlefield. The bridge crosses a shipping channel used by commercial vessels travelling into and out of the Sea of Azov, making the area important for regional trade and grain exports.
The collapse of a major section, particularly its supporting arch, raises the possibility that debris could obstruct the channel and complicate the movement of larger commercial vessels.
RUSSIA'S RETALIATORY ATTACKS ON KYIV
The Crimean Bridge operation unfolded alongside another intense round of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Russian strikes had damaged the city's Northern and Southern bridges, two important crossings over the Dnipro River. Parts of the metro system were also affected, while disruptions to electricity, heating and water supplies were reported.
The attacks prompted transport restrictions and forced residents to seek shelter as explosions were heard across the capital.
Russia also struck energy infrastructure.

agritech-0894ae77e4.headline: How India became a rice powerhouse - and why it's becoming a problem
agritech-0894ae77e4.fulltext:
[Text below is Deccan Herald's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Last Updated  IST
Sisonee, India: India has grown into a rice-producing powerhouse, thanks to crop-science advances and subsidies designed decades ago to keep the nation fed.
It's also generated a growing rice surplus – much of it exported – even as India's government shoulders the rising cost of subsidies.
A Reuters review of federal government communications with states and interviews with 10 officials and more than a dozen scientists show rising concern in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration about the fiscal strain of subsidising rice that's feeding people abroad as well as Indians at home.
Rice subsidies make up more than two-thirds of India's federal food subsidy bill, which has more than doubled in a decade to 2.28 trillion rupees ($24.1 billion) in 2025/26.
"In effect, we are using taxpayers' money to subsidise foreign consumers," said Ashok Gulati, an agricultural economist and former government adviser on crop prices. He said the surplus was being "dumped on global markets at prices that undercut competitors."
Even as poor rains due to El Nino are expected to deliver a lower Indian harvest in 2026/27, ample stocks mean the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) still forecasts Indian exports rising in the next two years.
The surplus stems in part from new rice varieties that have opened up swathes of flood-prone east India to reliable cultivation, helping boost national output by 50% in a decade to a record 154 million tons in 2025/26 – outstripping domestic consumption of 107 million tons in the nation of 1.4 billion people.
The rise has been supported by a federal rice subsidy system since the mid-1960s, when India struggled to feed itself. More recently, state governments have also offered so-called bonuses on top of the federal minimum price, lifting output further.
In 1965, the government told Indians to go without dinner one day a week because of inadequate harvests. Now, exports have doubled in a decade to 22.3 million tons in 2025, Indian grain accounts for 40% of the global rice trade and there is barely enough storage for the rising stocks.
"We have run out of space," said Navin Aggarwal, a private miller in Cuttack, in the east Indian state of Odisha, where production has surged. "We have been waiting for government agencies to lift the rice they have already bought from us."
'Unfair competition'
Under the subsidy system, the federal government sets a Minimum Support Price for rice each year, taking account of inputs ranging from labour to fertiliser costs, giving farmers an incentive to grow the grain. Rice-producing states often offer an additional sum on top, making rice more profitable.
The resulting surpluses have led to rising tensions between India's federal government and state administrations over those state bonuses, which add to rice overproduction and squeeze out crops, such as oilseeds and pulses, that need to be imported.
One senior federal food ministry official told Reuters that rice-producing states continue to pressure the ministry to buy more rice, calling the situation "exasperating".
Political tensions stretch beyond India. As India's exports climb, rival producers from Thailand and Vietnam to the United States have voiced growing frustration.
US President Donald Trump in December accused India of "dumping", or selling rice below cost. New Delhi, which is negotiating a trade deal with Washington, dismissed the charge, saying it sold expensive premium basmati rice to the US.
Trade body USA Rice said in April "unfair competition from bad actors like India" threatened US sales.
A USDA spokesperson told Reuters in a statement that Washington had "long raised concerns" about India's rice subsidy. US trade, commerce and White House officials did not respond to requests for comment.
Thailand, meanwhile, appealed for cooperation with India and Vietnam in 2025 to stop prices falling and, in October, Bangkok said India's large stocks added to pressure on Thai exporters.
Indian rice sells at a discount of about $110 a ton to benchmark Thai rice, which was trading around $497 per ton in mid-November.
Thai and Vietnamese officials did not respond to requests for comment. India's finance, agriculture, food and trade ministries also did not reply.
'We grow more rice than we can eat'
India's rice revolution has been fuelled by the Swarna-SUB1 grain, released for commercial use in 2009 by Indian researchers who combined the flood-tolerant FR13A variety with the widely used Swarna variety, known for high yields.
Most rice production traditionally came from north and northwest India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana. Now, the new variety has transformed harvests in flood-prone east India.
Chandramohan Yadav farms in the eastern state of Bihar. His village of Sisonee is near the Kosi River, known as the "River of Sorrows" for its devastating deluges.
"There were years when we barely grew enough rice to feed our family, and sometimes the floods wiped out the entire harvest," he said. "Now, we grow more rice than we can eat."
Production in Bihar surged 182% in the past 15 years to 8.75 million tons in 2025/26. In neighbouring Odisha, it rose 50% to 10.2 million tons.
Researchers are working on combining flood and drought tolerance into a single grain, helping farmers dependent on unpredictable monsoon rains, said Rameswar Sah, a senior scientist at state-run ICAR-Central Rice Research Institute.
New varieties are expected to add at least 10 million tons to output over the next five years, according to estimates cited by two scientists and two government officials.
A report by top government advisory body NITI Aayog, seen by Reuters, forecast total output would reach 171 million tons by 2036. But domestic demand would only rise to 110 million tons.
Faced with a growing surplus, the government has directed some rice towards ethanol production. But government rice stocks continue to climb, reaching a record 55.47 million tons on October 1, more than four times the target.
The federal food ministry said in September, in a document seen by Reuters, the government planned to add 13.1 million tons of storage capacity to address a "growing mismatch between procurement and offtake and regional imbalances."
Bhagwant Mann, chief minister of Punjab, urged the federal government in a September 29 letter to move 600,000 tons of government-bought rice harvested last year out of local storage to other warehouses – or risk a delay in buying the new harvest that could spark "unrest" among farmers.
State bonuses in government crosshairs
Farmers in India, where agriculture employs more than 40% of the workforce, have opposed any move to trim subsidies. A protest in 2020 and 2021 against farm laws that farmers feared would end the federal Minimum Support Price prompted the government to repeal the laws in November 2021.
Reluctant to adjust the federal subsidy, the government has tried to stop state bonuses. It has made little headway, as state governments fear a backlash from farmers at the ballot box if they rein in the handouts.
The federal food ministry approached the finance ministry three times in the past two years urging it to stop states from offering bonuses, three government sources said.
In a January 9 letter seen by Reuters, the finance ministry's Department of Expenditure urged states to align incentives with national priorities to grow other crops and said water-intensive rice was straining groundwater resources.
Importing oilseeds and pulses cost India $22.7 billion in 2025, up 120% in the past decade, while rice exports earned $12 billion, trade ministry data shows.
Experts say rice uses more fertiliser than oilseeds and pulses, adding to India's fertiliser subsidy bill, which is expected to exceed 3 trillion rupees ($31.8 billion) in 2026/27, four times the level of a decade ago, the fertiliser ministry estimated.
Food ministry officials also raised concerns about rice bonuses with state food officials in September 2025 and March 2026, four government sources said.
Abhishek Govilkar, head of agribusiness at BigMint consultancy, said convincing state officials to drop the bonuses won’t be easy.
"State governments see bonuses as a tool to win elections," he said, making it "difficult for the government to check its runaway expenditure."

other-interests-a18ee02857.headline: Just nine countries back pledge to tackle AI’s environmental footprint
other-interests-a18ee02857.fulltext:
Only nine countries have signed an international pledge to make AI greener, despite warnings at the COP31 climate summit that the technology’s growing energy demands threaten climate goals.
The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge was launched on 16 November at the summit in Turkey. Developed by the summit’s presidency and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), it intends to make AI more sustainable by encouraging cleaner energy use, more efficient data centres and greater transparency about the technology’s environmental footprint.
“AI and other frontier technologies are a double-edged sword,” said Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, at a press conference on 16 November. “The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones and put these technologies responsibly to work.”
Advertisement
But Ketan Joshi, an independent analyst researching AI’s climate impacts, questions that analogy. He says it conflates traditional machine learning, already used in applications such as weather forecasting, with energy-intensive generative AI. “You don’t need to have a giant, energy-hungry generative AI chatbot if you want to have better wind forecasting for a wind power developer,” he says.
The initiative comes as AI’s rapid expansion is placing growing pressure on electricity grids. According to the International Energy Agency, electricity consumption from AI-focused data centres increased by 50 per cent in 2025.
Joshi says there is little evidence that technology companies are building enough renewable energy capacity to meet this growing demand. Even companies that have invested heavily in renewables, such as Amazon and Google, are increasingly turning to fossil fuels to support their rapid expansion, he says.
The only countries to have endorsed the pledge so far are Andorra, Brazil, Colombia, Luxembourg, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Korea, Turkey and Uganda.
The pledge is voluntary, with no binding targets for cutting emissions or reducing energy consumption. It sets out four areas for action, including increasing the use of low- and zero-emission energy to power AI infrastructure, improving energy and water efficiency, and measuring the environmental impacts of AI systems. It also calls for greater financial and technical support to help developing countries use AI to tackle climate change.
However, the agreement leaves considerable room for interpretation. The call for using “low- and zero-emission energy”, for example, allows continued reliance on fossil gas rather than committing to renewable electricity.
Countries can also choose additional commitments, such as requiring AI companies to disclose their energy consumption and environmental impacts, or introducing sustainability requirements for data centres.
“I’m surprised that more countries haven’t signed up, given the pledge’s limited demands,” says Joshi. “It’s not a pledge that really strikes at the heart of the problem.” He argues that voluntary promises are unlikely to be sufficient without restrictions on the expansion of data centres and stronger AI regulation.
COP31 President Murat Kurum defended the initiative, saying the rapid growth of AI must be “powered and deployed responsibly, and used for the benefit of climate actions”. The ITU says progress on the pledge will be reviewed at annual UN climate summits until 2030, starting at COP32 next year.
Joshi fears the pledge could provide cover for continued expansion via fossil fuel sources. “I think we’re going to be going into an era of a return to greenwashing, a return to sort of empty promises,” he says. “What we really need is stronger and stricter regulation.”

world-1eb6c4f0c3.headline: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
world-1eb6c4f0c3.fulltext:
Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
- Published
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

US chip giant Nvidia doubled revenue in the third quarter to more than US$115 billion, the company reported on Tuesday while ruling out any return for ousted CEO Jensen Huang after a Chinese spy scandal.
The results, which beat expectations, came hours after Huang said he wanted his job back in the latest twist for the company at the centre of an AI boom that has propelled markets to record highs and boosted global economic growth.
Huang, a leading promoter of AI, stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a spy for Beijing.
Investors scoured the upbeat results for evidence that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” interim CEO Colette Kress said in a statement, her first since being appointed by the board last week.
She forecast stronger revenue growth of 75 per cent in next financial year, up from 70 per cent.
The recent upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia – which has lost US$700 billion in market value since the scandal broke – and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.
But his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and others for his return, and even US President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the espionage allegations.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in his first statement since his resignation.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
But Harvey Jones, the chair of the company’s board, slapped down the move, saying in an earnings call that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.
As the scandal deepened, Washington on Monday announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing.
The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.
The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.
The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.
His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying: “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”

climate-energy-8ab4d66d23.headline: Amazon to Invest $7 Billion in Indian Renewable Energy by 2030, Unveils 4 New Projects
climate-energy-8ab4d66d23.fulltext:
Amazon is set to significantly boost India's clean energy landscape with a planned $7 billion investment in renewable energy projects by 2030, adding to its existing commitments and unveiling four new wind and solar initiatives.
Key Points
- Amazon plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, bringing its total contracted investment to $11 billion.
- The company unveiled four new wind and solar projects in India with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts, including a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka.
- Once operational, Amazon's Indian renewable portfolio will exceed 2 GW, capable of powering over 3.5 million households annually.
- These investments contribute to Amazon's global goal of reducing the carbon intensity of its electricity operations by 65 per cent by 2030 and achieving net-zero carbon by 2040.
- Union Minister Pralhad Joshi welcomed the investment, highlighting its role in India's clean energy ambitions and economic growth.
Amazon on Tuesday announced plans to invest $7 billion (about Rs 65,393 crore) in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, in addition to the $4 billion already contracted, as it unveiled four new wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts.
The company said the investment makes it one of India's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.
New Projects and Capacity Expansion
The four initiatives consist of a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka-marking Amazon's largest contracted wind project in Asia to date-alongside a 200 MW hybrid solar-and-wind facility in the southern state, a 300 MW solar installation in Madhya Pradesh, and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan.
Secured through power purchase agreements (PPAs), the projects are part of Amazon's $4 billion investment in renewable energy projects already contracted in India, the company said.
Amazon stated that once operational, its Indian renewable portfolio will exceed 2 GW, enough to meet the annual power demands of more than 3.5 million households in the country.
Commitment to Carbon-Free Energy
The company's portfolio in India comprises a total of 57 projects, including 14 utility-scale wind and solar projects that add carbon-free energy to the grid and 43 on-site solar installations across its facilities.
The investments will also contribute to a new global goal announced by the company to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65 per cent by 2030.
Every unit of electricity the company consumes will be associated with 65 per cent fewer carbon emissions against a 2019 baseline, it said.
The company described the target as a milestone towards its goal of achieving net-zero carbon across operations by 2040.
Government and Global Perspective
Union minister for New and Renewable Energy, Education, Consumer Affairs and Food and Public Distribution, Pralhad Joshi, welcomed the investment.
"Such investments play an important role in advancing India's clean energy ambitions, strengthening energy security and supporting sustainable economic growth.
"They also demonstrate the growing confidence of global companies in India's renewable energy sector and its potential to attract long-term investment, create economic opportunities and accelerate the country's energy transition," he said.
Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon, said the company aims to help meet India's growing electricity demand and contribute to the country's goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2070.
Globally, Amazon is among the largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy, with more than 700 wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of over 40 GW, the company said.
