work-careers-ca6d16daa8.headline: US proposes sweeping changes to green card rules, raises employer compliance burden and tightens scrutiny
work-careers-ca6d16daa8.fulltext:
The US Department of Labour (DOL) has proposed a major overhaul of the employment-based green card process, introducing stricter recruitment requirements, tighter restrictions following layoffs and greater scrutiny of employers sponsoring foreign workers for permanent residence. The proposed changes to the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme would constitute its most significant revision in nearly 20 years, the department said.
PERM is a mandatory labour market test for most employment-based EB-2 and EB-3 green card applications, requiring sponsoring employers to demonstrate that qualified US workers are unavailable for the positions offered to foreign nationals.
“The proposed rule would represent the most significant revision of the PERM program since its inception,” said Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at global immigration law firm Fragomen.
The general view in industries, especially the technology sector, is that the extension of the minimum recruitment period will pose a major challenge. Wexler explained that under the proposed rule, sponsoring employers would have to advertise a job for at least 90 days. If they normally advertise similar jobs for longer than 90 days, they would have to follow that longer period. Currently, the minimum advertising period is 30 days.
The DOL says the proposed rule would require employers to level the playing field when recruiting workers by using the same channels and methods for advertising jobs.
Employers would have to advertise positions through state job orders, their own websites, job-search portals and social media platforms where these are customarily used. Job fairs and campus recruitment would also be included. Newspaper advertisements would no longer be mandatory, while advertisements would have to specify the offered salary or wage range.
Recently, Cloudera was barred from sponsoring foreign workers through PERM for two years following allegations that it deliberately excluded American applicants from certain technology jobs. According to a statement from the US Department of Justice, Cloudera created a separate recruitment process for seven positions earmarked for workers holding temporary visas. US applicants were allegedly directed to submit resumes to an email address that could not receive external messages. Under a settlement, the company agreed to establish a $1.4 million back-pay fund for affected workers and pay $600,000 in civil penalties.
“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” Keith Sonderling, Labour Secretary said. “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labour.”
Employers would also have to submit extensive supporting documents with every PERM application, including prevailing wage determinations, recruitment advertisements, detailed recruitment reports and resumes or applications of all US workers who applied. Currently, such documents are generally required only if an application is selected for audit.
“This significant process revision would result in a longer and more burdensome process, reviving many of the procedures and administrative requirements that PERM was designed to eliminate,” Wexler said.
The proposal also introduces a two-year restriction on approval of PERM applications if an employer has laid off workers in the same or a related occupation in the same area of intended employment. The rule also creates ongoing reporting and US worker consideration requirements for layoffs that occur even after the PERM application is filed.
Another major change is the proposed elimination of Schedule A, which currently exempts professional nurses, physical therapists and individuals with exceptional ability in the arts and sciences from the labour market test.
The proposed elimination of Schedule A could also have significant implications for the US healthcare sector. The American Hospital Association had previously urged the DOL to retain nurses and physical therapists on the shortage occupation list, while also calling for medical doctors to be added to the list.
The rules would also expand workplace notice requirements, including at third-party worksites, and introduce stricter employer declarations on wages, recruitment practices and non-discrimination. Recruitment that is less accessible or less favourable to US workers would be presumed to be in bad faith, according to the proposal, and could independently lead to denial.
The proposal comes amid a wider crackdown on employment-based immigration. In October, the US administration suspended eight companies, viz: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini — from the PERM programme. Separately, IBM announced on November 10 that it would discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of roles in its Consulting division.
The proposal is open for a 60-day public comment period. The rulemaking process is expected to take several months. The changes will not take effect until the regulation is finalised.

indian-startups-46852824f6.headline: Google Begins Rolling Out Personal AI Assistant, Tasks, In India
indian-startups-46852824f6.fulltext: Big tech giant Google has begun rolling out its new agentic AI assistant Tasks, formerly Gemini Sparks, to users in India. In a blogpost, Josh Woodward, the vice-president of Google Labs and the Gemini app, said that the new feature will enable users to assign tasks to the AI assistant, including making calls, booking appointments, comparing products and completing purchases. The service comes bundled for free with Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. “Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model,” said Woodward. It is pertinent to note that Tasks was reportedly initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, an agentic AI helper. It was subsequently expanded to the US-based subscribers of the Google AI Ultra tier. Google is now rolling out this feature for free in six markets. Unlike Gemini’s Chat that only generates responses to a user’s queries, Tasks goes one step further and enables the chatbot to perform basic functions. With the rollout, Google could be looking to expand the role of AI assistants beyond answering questions to embedding them in daily life. In his blog post, Woodward noted that Gemini can draw on information already available within Google services, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, files and payment cards, to carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. With Tasks, he also said that Gemini can call businesses, wait through hold periods, identify available appointment slots and add bookings to a user’s calendar. Under the hood, Gemini uses the agent payments protocol (AP2) to enable Tasks to make purchases online. Going forward, the big tech giant said that it plans to integrate the universal commerce protocol (UCP) into Gemini to further streamline the checkout experience. Google also said that it is working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to enable tokenised card transactions via Tasks. However, the big tech juggernaut did not specify whether partnerships extend to India too. That said, India’s inclusion in the initial rollout gives Google a large market to test consumer adoption of the personal AI assistant feature. To further scale the rollout, Google has also invited app developers to join its Connected Apps Platform, which could pave the way for Indian consumer, fintech, travel tech and foodtech brands to build task-based third-party integrations with the assistant. These features could make Gemini Tasks a channel for online shopping, bill payments and routine purchases. However, adoption will depend on the availability of supported merchants, payment methods and third-party apps in the country. There appears to be no clarity on this front. The launch is part of a broader wave of big tech giants rolling out personal AI assistants to capture the masses. In September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg showcased the company’s new offering called Muse, which allows an AI agent to send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. Prior to this, OpenAI also introduced Dots that can draft board meeting decks, conduct background research, and handle multi-step project management. xAI has also been developing Grok Bot, which sees cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. Microsoft is also pursuing agents, built on OpenClaw, which can function as digital teammates. Back home, Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform, launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps.

india-9195fb7d09.headline: India's AI data centre expansion faces internal electrical bottlenecks: Fluke study
india-9195fb7d09.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: India’s ambitions to become a major hub for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre infrastructure face significant operational hurdles, according to a new Fluke Corporation study. While operators look to scale capacity, gaps in internal electrical systems are emerging as a critical bottleneck for deploying higher-density AI workloads.Fluke commissioned the study on behalf of Censuswide, which surveyed 1,300 data centre operators and professionals across India, the US, the UK, Germany, France, and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. In India, 75% of operators experienced electrical or power-system issues in the past year.Furthermore, only 23% of Indian data centre operators consider their existing electrical infrastructure fully prepared for higher-density AI workloads. These findings highlight growing pressure on facility infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates and computing demands become increasingly power-intensive.External supply constraints are compounding these internal challenges, with 79% of Indian operators stating that access to sufficient power and grid capacity moderately or severely limits expansion. Operators report an average 13-month wait to secure additional grid connections or power capacity for AI and GPU-related growth."The industry has spent years asking where the power will come from. But our findings show that the focus should also be on how effectively data centres can use the power they already have," said Parker Burke, president of Fluke. "As AI drives unprecedented demand for computing capacity, the electrical infrastructure inside data centres is becoming a critical bottleneck. Without addressing this last-mile challenge, the industry risks having the power to expand, but not the infrastructure to deliver."Operational disruptions are already impacting deployment timelines across the sector. Nearly one-third (31%) of Indian operators report that power-quality issues, such as voltage fluctuations, harmonics, and electrical disturbances, have reduced their ability to deploy or operate high-density AI or GPU workloads.Additionally, 23% of operators noted that electrical problems are identified only after performance degradation, equipment failure, or downtime has already occurred. This reactive posture underscores the need for continuous power-quality monitoring, thermal inspections, and preventive maintenance to curb unplanned outages.On the monitoring front, 53% of Indian operators report comprehensive or extensive real-time visibility across critical electrical systems, placing the country ahead of the 45% global average. However, the report notes that operators must build upon these capabilities to detect faults before they disrupt operations.Workforce constraints present another hurdle to scaling capacity. More than half of Indian operators (56%) say recruiting qualified electrical technicians has become more difficult, while 31% report that electrical skills shortages have delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity."Grid constraints are largely outside an operator's control. What is within their control is how effectively they monitor, maintain and manage the electrical infrastructure they already have," Burke added. "Greater visibility into electrical systems and a proactive approach to maintenance will be increasingly important as operators look to maximize existing capacity, reduce disruption and support growing AI demand."

India’s deeptech funding record faces a test of scale: Speciale Invest
India’s deeptech funding hit $914 million in 2025, but limited growth capital, manufacturing dependencies and weak commercialisation pathways continue to hinder startups from scaling.
India’s deeptech companies raised $914 million in 257 rounds in 2025, 34 times the 2016 level. The harder test is turning research and prototypes into commercial products, notes Speciale Invest’s report, India’s Deep Tech Revolution - From the Lab to Growth and Exits.
Using Tracxn data through August 31 2026, the study covers 8,293 private companies worldwide, including 482 in India. India accounted for 12.8% of deeptech funding rounds in 2025 but received 1.6% of the capital.
For every 100 seed rounds, India had 23 Series A or B rounds, against 105 globally. Separately, there was one late-stage or private-equity round per 100 Indian seed rounds, against 26 worldwide. Both measures point to funding thinning as companies mature.
Sectoral advantages are uneven. Space firms can tap ISRO testing facilities and suppliers, while life-sciences ventures can draw on India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing base. Private participation in space has widened since 2020 reforms. Registered space startups rose from one in 2014 to about 440 by August 2026.
In July, Skyroot’s Vikram-I became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit from Indian soil. It was a milestone, though one launch does not establish a repeatable commercial business.
The report says battery makers still rely on imported cells and materials. Separately, Exide commissioned phase one of a 6 GWh Bengaluru cell plant in September. Semiconductor developers remain reliant on overseas fabrication and packaging. Semicon 2.0, approved in July with Rs 1,27,500 crore, aims to expand domestic capacity; the first fab is due in 2028.
The six-year Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Scheme aims to finance high-risk technology. By July 2026, the Technology Development Board had approved 22 projects with Rs 2,192 crore in support. Assistance is mainly through low-interest long-term loans, equity and equity-linked instruments, rather than standard grants.
Turning a successful pilot, or customer trial, into an order remains difficult. Vishesh Rajaram, managing partner at Speciale Invest, said, “Large companies and public-sector buyers can help turn those trials into commercial orders by agreeing upfront on what a pilot must prove and when they’ll make a purchase decision. A first order lets a startup plan production and commit to suppliers.”
Growth capital is smaller too. Indian Series A and B rounds averaged $11.5 million from January to August 2026, against $55.5 million globally, said Vishnu Rajeev, investment partner at Speciale Invest.
“That gap matters when a founder needs to qualify a product with a major customer or commission a production line before commercial revenue is predictable, Rajeev adds. He argues funding should match milestone costs, with project finance once customers make firm commitments.
The report urges faster funding decisions, shared testing facilities, more domestic Series B and C investors, and plant finance before pilots end. It also considers listings, acquisitions, licensing and secondary share sales as exit routes.
Deeptech needs not just research funding, but reliable customers and patient growth capital.

Key Highlights
- Indian deep tech companies raised funding in 257 rounds in 2025. Total funding reached 34 times the 2016 level.
- For every 100 deep tech seed rounds in 2025, India recorded one late-stage or private equity round, compared with 26 globally.
- Space and life sciences startups can draw on India’s established testing and manufacturing infrastructure.
- The report calls for more domestic growth capital and clearer routes from successful pilots to purchase orders.
Chennai / Bengaluru, India, November 16th — Speciale Invest today released the second edition of India’s Deep Tech Revolution, titled From the Lab to Growth and Exits. Indian deep tech companies in the study raised $914 million in 2025. The report examines what it takes to move from a working prototype to commercial production and how founders and investors can realise returns.
Sectors Reaching Commercial Scale
Space startups can draw on testing facilities and suppliers associated with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). The report cites Agnikul Cosmos’s launch from India’s first private launchpad, built with ISRO support. Life sciences startups can build on India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing base. Semiconductor developers still rely on overseas fabrication and packaging, and battery companies depend on imported cells and materials.
Public Funding and First Customers
The report identifies the government’s ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Fund as a source of finance for companies moving towards commercial deployment. It records ₹2,192 crore for 22 projects in the fund’s first round through the Technology Development Board.
The report also tracks faculty at the IITs and IISc turning research into companies. It cites NTPC and Indian Oil’s engagement with energy storage startup Sthyr Energy as an example of how large public-sector companies are working with startups.
The Funding Gap After Seed
India accounted for 12.8% of global deep tech funding rounds in 2025 and 1.6% of the capital invested. For every 100 seed rounds, India recorded 23 Series A or B rounds, compared with 105 globally. Startups moving from a pilot to commercial production also face slow grant decisions and procurement requirements designed for established suppliers.
Recommendations for Growth and Exits
The report calls on government agencies to publish timelines for funding decisions, institutions to expand access to shared testing facilities, and domestic funds to lead more Series B and C rounds. It recommends that founders line up financing for a first plant before a pilot ends. It also examines public listings, strategic acquisitions, licensing and secondary share sales as ways to realise value.
Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner at Speciale Invest, said, “More Indian deep tech startups are running pilots with customers. Large companies and public-sector buyers can help turn those trials into commercial orders by agreeing upfront on what a pilot must prove and when they’ll make a purchase decision. A first order lets a startup plan production and commit to suppliers. Delivering that order gives the company a reference it can take to its next customer, in India or abroad.”
Vishnu Rajeev, Investment Partner at Speciale Invest, said, “From January to August 2026, deep tech Series A and B rounds averaged $11.5 million in India and $55.5 million globally. That gap matters when a founder needs to qualify a product with a major customer or commission a production line before commercial revenue is predictable. Investors can size a round around the time and cost of reaching the next milestone and reserve capital to follow on as the company delivers. Once customers make firm purchase commitments, project finance can help fund a first commercial plant alongside equity.”
The funding analysis draws on Tracxn data through 31 August 2026. It covers 8,293 privately held companies globally, including 482 in India, that met the report’s criteria for sector, business model and equity funding.
About Speciale Invest
Speciale Invest is an Indian venture capital firm founded in 2017 by Vishesh Rajaram and Arjun Rao. It backs deep tech companies from pre-seed through growth across sectors including space, energy transition, advanced manufacturing, computing and life sciences.

beyond-your-beat-b854b7f468.headline: Ukraine strikes Putin's prized Crimean Bridge, destroys central road section ahead of US-China meet
beyond-your-beat-b854b7f468.fulltext:
Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea on Tuesday, destroying its central road section and sending part of the structure crashing into the sea. The attack, carried out using drones and missiles, has disrupted a key supply route for Russian forces and comes two days before President Vladimir 
Putin
 is due to meet the leaders of China and the US.
Footage show that the bridge's main road arch had collapsed into the sea, leaving a large gap in the structure. Russian officials said road traffic had been suspended, while rail services had partly resumed.
The damage has disrupted a direct supply route to Crimea, increasing Russia's reliance on routes through occupied mainland Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" that had been weeks in the making. He said it was carried out by the Ukraine Security Service along with all of Ukraine's forces.
"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges," Zelenskyy said. "We are ... reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began."
In his video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had repeatedly urged Moscow to stop attacking infrastructure but Russia had continued to escalate the conflict.
"We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, cities and villages, energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. 
Enough of war," Zelenskyy said, as cited by Reuters. "But every time Russia chooses further escalation."
Meanwhile, Kremlin said that it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
Why the Crimean Bridge matters to Russia
The 19-km (12-mile) bridge is a major road and rail connection between Russia and occupied Crimea. It also serves as a route for Russian soldiers travelling towards the front line, making it an important link for Moscow's military operations.
Ukraine has targeted the bridge several times but has struggled to shut it down permanently. The latest attack has damaged a key section and disrupted road traffic, while rail services have only partly resumed.
Kyiv has also been targeting Russian oil refineries and depots to increase the economic cost of the war. Striking the bridge is another attempt to put pressure on Putin, this time by raising the political cost of the conflict.
Putin's personal project
The bridge, built in 2014, has particular significance for Putin. It is widely seen in both Russia and Ukraine as the Russian president's personal project and a symbol of Moscow's control over the peninsula.
The $3.6 billion (£2.7 billion) infrastructure project was built by Arkady Rotenberg, a tycoon and close friend of Putin. The Russian president personally inaugurated it in May 2018 by driving a lorry across it.
The timing of the attack is also significant, coming just two days before Putin is due to meet the leaders of China and the US. The damage could overshadow his return to the international spotlight.
Meanwhile, in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges, key crossings over the Dnipro River. Both had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.

world-d9f6d74fe1.headline: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
world-d9f6d74fe1.fulltext:
Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.
The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe.
The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.
Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.
That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.
Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.
It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.
Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.
Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.
Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.
If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.
A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.
The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.
Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.
“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.

agritech-ebe9010fd1.headline: How India became a rice powerhouse and why it’s becoming a problem
agritech-ebe9010fd1.fulltext:
World
How India became a rice powerhouse and why it’s becoming a problem
Advances in crop science and decades of subsidies have driven Indian rice production to record levels, but mounting surpluses are straining public finances, storage capacity and relations with competing exporters.
Reuters
India has become a rice-producing powerhouse, thanks to advances in crop science and subsidies introduced decades ago to ensure the country could feed itself.
But the transformation has also created a growing surplus, much of which is exported, even as the government faces mounting costs from subsidising production.
A Reuters review of federal government communications with state governments and interviews with 10 officials and more than a dozen scientists reveal growing concern within Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration over the financial burden of subsidising rice that feeds consumers abroad as well as at home.
Rice subsidies account for more than two-thirds of India’s federal food subsidy bill, which has more than doubled in a decade to 2.28 trillion rupees ($24.1 billion) in 2025/26.
“In effect, we are using taxpayers’ money to subsidise foreign consumers,” said Ashok Gulati, an agricultural economist and former government adviser on crop prices. He said the surplus was being “dumped on global markets at prices that undercut competitors”.
Even as poor rainfall linked to El Niño is expected to result in a smaller harvest in 2026/27, ample stocks mean the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) still forecasts an increase in Indian exports over the next two years.
The surplus stems partly from new rice varieties that have made large areas of flood-prone eastern India suitable for reliable cultivation. This has helped raise national output by 50 percent in a decade, to a record 154 million tonnes in 2025/26, well above domestic consumption of 107 million tonnes in the country of 1.4 billion people.
The increase has been supported by a federal rice subsidy system introduced in the mid-1960s, when India struggled to feed its population. More recently, state governments have also offered bonuses on top of the federal minimum support price, further encouraging production.
In 1965, the government urged Indians to skip dinner one day a week because of poor harvests. Today, rice exports have doubled in a decade to 22.3 million tonnes in 2025. Indian grain accounts for 40 percent of global rice trade, while storage space for the growing stocks is running out.
“We have run out of space,” said Navin Aggarwal, a private miller in Cuttack, in the eastern state of Odisha, where production has surged. “We have been waiting for government agencies to lift the rice they have already bought from us.”
‘Unfair competition’
Under the subsidy system, the federal government sets a minimum support price for rice every year, taking into account production costs, including labour and fertiliser. The guaranteed price gives farmers an incentive to grow the crop. Rice-producing states often offer additional payments, making cultivation even more profitable.
The resulting surpluses have fuelled tensions between the federal government and state administrations over these bonuses. They encourage further rice production, leaving less land for crops such as oilseeds and pulses, which India needs to import.
One senior federal food ministry official told Reuters that rice-producing states continued to pressure the ministry to purchase more rice, describing the situation as “exasperating”.
The tensions extend beyond India. As Indian exports rise, competing producers, from Thailand and Vietnam to the United States, have voiced growing frustration.
US President Donald Trump accused India in December of “dumping” rice, or selling it below cost. New Delhi, which is negotiating a trade deal with Washington, rejected the allegation, saying it exports premium-priced basmati rice to the United States.
Trade body USA Rice said in April that “unfair competition from bad actors like India” threatened US sales.
A US Department of Agriculture spokesperson told Reuters in a statement that Washington had “long raised concerns” about India’s rice subsidies. US trade, commerce and White House officials did not respond to requests for comment.
Thailand, meanwhile, called for cooperation with India and Vietnam in 2025 to prevent prices from falling. In October, Bangkok said India's large stocks were adding to pressure on Thai exporters.
Indian rice sells at a discount of about $110 per tonne compared with benchmark Thai rice, which was trading at around $497 per tonne in mid-November.
Thai and Vietnamese officials did not respond to requests for comment. India’s finance, agriculture, food and trade ministries also did not reply.
‘We grow more rice than we can eat’
India’s rice revolution has been driven in part by Swarna-SUB1, a variety released for commercial cultivation in 2009 by Indian researchers. They developed it by combining the flood-tolerant FR13A variety with the widely cultivated, high-yielding Swarna variety.
Traditionally, most rice production came from northern and north-western India, particularly Punjab and Haryana. The new variety has since transformed cultivation in flood-prone eastern India.
Chandramohan Yadav is a farmer in Bihar, in eastern India. His village, Sisonee, lies near the Kosi River, known as the “River of Sorrows” because of its devastating floods.
Rice production in Bihar rose 182 percent over the past 15 years to 8.75 million tonnes in 2025/26. In neighbouring Odisha, output increased 50 percent to 10.2 million tonnes.
Researchers are working to develop a variety that combines flood and drought tolerance, which would help farmers dependent on increasingly unpredictable monsoon rains, said Rameswar Sah, a senior scientist at the state-run ICAR-Central Rice Research Institute.
New varieties are expected to add at least 10 million tonnes to national output over the next five years, according to estimates cited by two scientists and two government officials.
A report by NITI Aayog, the government’s top policy advisory body, seen by Reuters, projected that total production would reach 171 million tonnes by 2036. Domestic demand, however, would rise only to 110 million tonnes.
Faced with the growing surplus, the government has directed some rice towards ethanol production. But government stocks continue to rise, reaching a record 55.47 million tonnes on October 1, more than four times the official target.
In a document seen by Reuters, the federal food ministry said in September that the government planned to add 13.1 million tonnes of storage capacity to address a “growing mismatch between procurement and offtake and regional imbalances”.
Bhagwant Mann, chief minister of Punjab, urged the federal government in a September 29 letter to move 600,000 tonnes of government-purchased rice from the previous year’s harvest to other warehouses. Otherwise, he warned, delays in purchasing the new harvest could trigger “unrest” among farmers.
State bonuses in government crosshairs
Farmers in India, where agriculture employs more than 40 percent of the workforce, have opposed any move to reduce subsidies. Protests in 2020 and 2021 against farm laws, which farmers feared would end the federal minimum support price system, forced the government to repeal the legislation in November 2021.
Unwilling to overhaul the federal subsidy system, the government has sought to curb additional payments offered by state governments. It has made little progress, as state administrations fear electoral backlash if they withdraw the incentives.
The federal food ministry approached the finance ministry three times over the past two years, urging it to prevent states from offering bonuses, three government sources said.
In a January 9 letter seen by Reuters, the finance ministry’s Department of Expenditure urged states to align their incentives with national priorities by encouraging the cultivation of other crops. It also warned that water-intensive rice cultivation was putting pressure on groundwater resources.
India spent $22.7 billion on importing oilseeds and pulses in 2025, a 120 percent increase over the past decade. Rice exports, meanwhile, earned the country $12 billion, according to trade ministry data.
Experts say rice cultivation requires more fertiliser than oilseeds and pulses, adding to India’s fertiliser subsidy burden. The fertiliser ministry estimates that the bill will exceed 3 trillion rupees ($31.8 billion) in 2026/27, four times its level a decade ago.
Food ministry officials also raised concerns about rice bonuses with state food officials in September 2025 and March 2026, four government sources said.
Abhishek Govilkar, head of agribusiness at consultancy BigMint, said persuading state officials to scrap the bonuses would not be easy.
“State governments see bonuses as a tool to win elections,” he said, making it “difficult for the government to check its runaway expenditure”.

world-bfcaf275b2.headline: Nvidia partner Megaspeed being investigated by US government over chip exports
world-bfcaf275b2.fulltext:
US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
- Published
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

agritech-c8ead4dde5.headline: ICRA sees India’s Q2FY27 GDP growth at 7.5% despite global, monsoon headwinds
agritech-c8ead4dde5.fulltext:
ICRA sees India’s Q2FY27 GDP growth at 7.5% despite global, monsoon headwinds
India’s economic growth is expected to remain resilient at 7.5% in the July-September quarter of FY27, despite external headwinds and an uneven monsoon, according to a projection by rating agency ICRA. However, the growth rate is likely to moderate from 7.8% recorded in the April-June quarter, marking a five-quarter low.
The anticipated moderation is expected to be broad-based, led by a sharp slowdown in agriculture and a relatively mild deceleration in industrial and services activity. ICRA estimates agricultural gross value added (GVA) growth to fall to 0.2% in Q2FY27 from 3.6% in Q1FY27. Industrial GVA growth is projected to ease to 7.2% from 7.7% while services GVA growth is expected to moderate to 9.1% from 10%.
Overall GVA growth is likely to decline to 7.2% in Q2FY27 from 8.2% in the previous quarter. GDP growth, however, is expected to be around 0.3 percentage points higher, supported by a healthy expansion in net indirect taxes on products. “The robustness in high-frequency data across the industrial and services sectors for Q2FY27 portends healthy economic growth in these segments in the quarter ending September 2026, belying sustained external headwinds. However, sub-par monsoons are expected to have weighed on agri GVA growth in the quarter, amid the dip in kharif sowing and a likely adverse impact on crop yields,” said Aditi Nayar, chief economist and head of research and outreach at ICRA.
The projected GDP growth of 7.5% would also exceed the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee's forecast of 7.2% for the quarter.
Manufacturing holds up, mining remains a drag
Industrial activity is expected to remain a key growth driver, supported by resilient manufacturing and construction activity. ICRA estimates manufacturing GVA growth at around 8.2% in Q2FY27, marginally lower than 9.2% in Q1FY27.
The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) indicates that manufacturing output growth accelerated to a series-high of 8.1% in Q2FY27 from 6.9% in the preceding quarter. Growth improved across 14 of the 23 manufacturing sub-segments, with automobile-related industries witnessing strong momentum.
Output of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers expanded 22.7%, compared with 15.3% in Q1FY27. Growth in other transport equipment accelerated to 24.2% from 19.5% while electrical equipment output rose 31.8% against 27% in the previous quarter. Output of other non-metallic mineral products grew 11.6%, compared with 7.6%.
Financial results of 895 listed manufacturing companies also indicated an acceleration in aggregate revenue growth. Their combined profit after tax returned to healthy year-on-year growth after contracting in Q1FY27, supported partly by a sharp improvement in the oil refining segment. However, mining continued to weigh on industrial performance. Mining output contracted 3.9% in Q2FY27, compared with a 1.2% decline in Q1FY27.
Services remain strong; agriculture faces pressure
The services sector is expected to retain its growth momentum, although its GVA expansion is projected to moderate to 9.1% in Q2FY27 from 10% in Q1FY27. Most high-frequency indicators covering trade, hotels, transport, communication, broadcasting, financial, real estate and professional services showed improved performance during the quarter.
Agriculture is likely to face the sharpest slowdown. Kharif sowing area declined 1% from year-ago levels, led by a 3.5% contraction in rice acreage. States including Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu witnessed significant declines amid below-normal rainfall during the southwest monsoon season. Uneven distribution of rainfall is also likely to have affected crop yields.
FY27 growth pegged at 7.1%
While economic activity remained unexpectedly resilient in the first half of FY27 despite global headwinds, ICRA expects growth to moderate in the second half. Deficient rainfall, rising inflation and elevated input costs could weigh on consumption demand and corporate margins, respectively. The high base effect associated with GST rate rationalisation is also expected to influence the growth trajectory.
“While trends for H1FY27 were quite healthy and unexpectedly resilient against the global headwinds, ICRA expects GDP growth to moderate in H2FY27,” Nayar added.

global-economics-cbb2177a53.headline: Nvidia’s Huang signals willingness to return as CEO; board sets up national security panel
global-economics-cbb2177a53.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-cbb2177a53.fulltext:
Updated - November 17, 2026  at 11:06 PM.
Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned from the chipmaker last week under a cloud of scandal, said on Tuesday he "would be honored" to come back as CEO if the board decided his return would be in the best interest of shareholders and employees.
"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in his first public statement since he resigned on November 12 over revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the chip firm's China business.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation," he said.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Huang's statement. Nvidia shares pared some declines and were last down 1%.
Earlier in the day Nvidia created a board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls, its first major governance move since Huang left.
Huang's relationships, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China, have raised questions about whether Nvidia's oversight kept pace with its rapid growth and increasing importance to US national security. The crisis had erased more than $400 billion from the company's market value by Monday's close.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee.
US President Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea.
The committee's creation comes a day after the Trump administration said it would further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips from companies including Nvidia, as Trump headed to China for talks with President Xi Jinping.
Washington has for years sought to curb Beijing's access to Nvidia's most advanced processors, putting the company's China business at the center of tensions over national security, trade and US technological leadership.
Chinese companies, however, have repeatedly found ways around the restrictions, while Huang had advocated allowing more chip exports to China.
US officials had raised concerns about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive and controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence agencies suspect has links to Chinese intelligence.
Megaspeed has been under investigation over the possible diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China and potential export-control violations. The company has denied wrongdoing.
Nvidia said the new committee will oversee its national security and global trade compliance programs and work with independent legal, national security and trade-compliance experts.
The company's National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report to the committee, while interim CEO Colette Kress will oversee day-to-day operations. The committee plans to meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive sessions.
Nvidia did not have a chief compliance officer, according to its 2026 proxy statement.
It was not immediately clear whether the committee was created in response to the revelations about Huang's affairs. Nvidia did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
While major technology companies including Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft have board committees overseeing areas such as regulatory compliance, cybersecurity, privacy and strategy, Nvidia's new panel has a narrower mandate focused on national security and export controls, a structure more commonly associated with aerospace and defense companies.
"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said.
Nvidia has also warned chip buyers in recent months that the proposed US Remote Access Security Act could expose the company and its customers to legal risks by expanding Washington's oversight of Chinese companies' access to AI chips through cloud services, CNBC reported on Tuesday.
Huang's daughter Madison Huang, who is a senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, was closely involved in shaping the public defence of the company's ties to Megaspeed, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. She did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
The company is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Tuesday.
